title: Syllabus
text:
Textbook
This website will serve as the primary text for this course. While the course is an introductory one in R (and Excel), below are two authoritative texts in the subject of data science and modeling/machine learning in R with {tidyverse} and {tidymodels} packages.

R for Data Science (2e) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, Garret Grolemund and Hadley Wickham
Tidy Modeling with R by Max Kuhn and Julia Silge

An excellent elementary statistics text written with R as its companion programming language:

Introduction to Modern Statistics (2e) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Description
Use Excel and R to perform data manipulation, data visualization, and basic statistical analysis in the natural and social sciences.

title: Syllabus
text:
Prerequisite
COR 14X or equivalent, or instructor’s permission

title: Syllabus
text:
Expected Student Learning Outcomes
Upon completion of the course requirements, students will be able to:

Input, save, and import/export data in Excel and R.
Install and load R packages; write R code using the IDE Positron.
Write clean and readable R code in Quarto, an open-source scientific and technical publishing system.
Perform data wrangling using the {dplyr} package.
Calculate summary statistics in Excel and R.
Create data visualizations in Excel and using the {ggplot2} package.
Perform linear regression, \(\chi^2\)-test, \(t\)-test, ANOVA, and Kruskal–Wallis tests in Excel and R.

title: Syllabus
text:
Method of Instruction.
Lectures and in-class activities are primary means of instruction in this course. Students are expected to be active participants.

title: Syllabus
text:
Methods of Assessment.

1. Participation

Setting up and maintaining effective project workflows and file management are critical to data science best practices.
You will submit screenshots (not pictures from your phone) every week to show that you keep up with these practices.
Participation counts for 5% of the final grade.



2. Homework

Homework assignments will be given on a weekly basis.
Late homework will be penalized at a rate of 10% per calendar day after the due date.
Homework accounts for 20% of the final grade.



3. Quizzes

Quizzes will be administered approximately once per week.
Quizzes constitute 10% of the final grade.



4. Projects

Three group projects will be assigned throughout the semester, each covering a major course topic. Each project is worth 15% of the final grade.
A final group project will be due at the end of the semester. You will deliver a 15-minute presentation for the this project. It is worth 20% of the final grade.

title: Syllabus
text:
Attendance Policy
Attendance is an important part of your personal responsibility in this course. Missing more than 20% (8 classes) may result in withdrawal from the course by the professor, with a grade of “W” or “WF”, in accordance with the Academic Calendar.

title: Syllabus
text:
Expectations

If you own a laptop, you are expected to bring it to class each day, fully charged so that it will last the entire class session.
Students are expected to communicate with the professor using their official Flagler College email account. Messages sent from personal email addresses will not receive a response.
All email communication should be conducted in a professional manner, including the use of proper email etiquette and a clear, informative subject line.
Please allow up to 24 hours for a response, excluding weekends and holidays.

title: Syllabus
text:
Artificial Intelligence Tools Policy.

1. Acceptable Use of AI Tools
The use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, is permitted in this course for the following activities:

Brainstorming and refining ideas.
Fine-tuning research questions for projects.
Finding information relating to a topic of interest.
Drafting outlines to organize thoughts.
Checking spelling, grammar, and style.



2. Unacceptable Use of AI Tools.
The use of generative AI tools is not permitted in this course for the following activities.

Completing assignments, quizzes, or projects entirely or primarily using generative AI.

You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query. Your use of AI tools must be properly documented and cited in accordance with the college’s policy on academic honesty. Any assignment, quiz, or project that is found to have used generative AI tools in an unauthorized way will receive a grade of 0% for the first offense. A second offense will result in a grade of WF for this course. If you are unsure whether the use of an AI tool is permitted, please consult the professor for guidance or clarification.

text: We often collect and record data in units that are most convenient to us. However, these units may not always be the ones we need when performing calculations. For example, we may record the lengths of tortoises in inches but later need to convert these values to centimeters or meters. In instances such as this, we can write basic formulas to transform existing data.

title: Section 1.1: Introduction to Excel
text:
Let us now open the Excel app.

WindowsmacOS


To open Excel in Windows, type in “Excel” in the Windows search bar and click on the Excel icon to open the app. Alternatively, you can press the Windows key to bring up the search bar in the Start Menu.







To open Excel in macOS, open the Spotlight search bar by pressing Cmd + Space, then type in “Excel”.








Excel will first open to its template window. To begin data entry, double click on Blank Workbook.





There are two main parts to each Excel spreadsheet: the sheets and the Ribbon.

The sheet is the area where you enter and view data, including values and formulas.
The Ribbon provides shortcuts to Excel commands and tools, making it easier to format, organize, and analyze your spreadsheet.



The Ribbon
The row above the Ribbon are the Tabs, it is a menu of different groups of commands. An icon in the Ribbon is called a command. Sometimes a command icon has a dropdown menu which displays more commands.



The Sheet
A sheet is a spreadsheet made up of columns and rows. Each individual rectangle within the sheet is called a cell. Cells are where you enter data, such as values and formulas.

Columns are labeled using the English alphabet: A, B, C, etc.
Rows are labeled with numbers: 1, 2, 3, etc.

Each cell is identified by its column letter and row number, such as A1 or C5. When a cell is highlighted, its reference value is displayed in the Name Box.

Each sheet is labeled by the sheet tab at the bottom of each sheet.

To rename a sheet, right click (or click with two fingers) to bring up the context menu and select Rename.



Working with Multiple Sheets
It is possible to work with multiple datasets by saving them on separate sheets within the same Excel workbook. There are several ways to add a new sheet in the current workbook. The easiest method is to click on the “+” symbol to the right of the sheet name tab.

title: Section 0.1: Files, Folders, and File Types
text:
A sound file management system is an important part of modern data science. Throughout this course, you will create, download, open, modify, and save many different types of files. Keeping these files organized makes it easier for you and your collaborators to locate data, understand your workflow, and reproduce your analyses.
In this chapter, we will introduce the basic terminology of file management and examine how files and folders are organized in Windows and macOS. We will also discuss file paths, file extensions, and a few practical conventions for keeping your work organized.

title: Section 0.1: Files, Folders, and File Types
text:
1. Files and Folders

What is a file?
A file is a named collection of information stored on a computer. A file might contain text, a spreadsheet, a picture, a program, or data used in an analysis.
Examples include:

lecture_notes.qmd — a Quarto document.
penguins.csv — a comma-separated values data file.
results.xlsx — an Excel workbook.
plot.png — an image.
analysis.R — an R script.

The filename helps you identify the file’s purpose. In many cases, the filename also includes a file extension, such as .csv or .xlsx, which indicates the file type.


What is a folder?
A folder is a container used to organize files and other folders. A folder inside another folder is often called a subfolder. Folders can be arranged in a hierarchy, allowing related files to be grouped together.
For example, a course might use a structure like this:
CIS_351/
├── Week_01/
│   ├── week_01_lecture.qmd
│   └── notes.pdf
├── Week_02/
│   ├── penguins.csv
│   └── week_02_lecture.qmd
└── Homework/
    └── assignment_01.qmd
This is a text representation of a folder structure. The exact appearance of folders and files differs between operating systems, but the basic idea is the same: folders help you organize related files.


Why organization matters
A consistent folder structure helps you:

Find files again after saving or downloading them.
Keep raw data separate from cleaned data, code, and results.
Avoid accidentally editing or overwriting the wrong file.
Share a project with classmates or collaborators.
Make your analysis easier to understand and reproduce.

For data analysis, it is especially helpful to keep all files for a project in one main project folder, with clearly named subfolders when needed.

title: Section 0.1: Files, Folders, and File Types
section: 2. Finding Files in Windows and macOS
text:
2. Finding Files in Windows and macOS
Windows and macOS use different names for their main file-management applications.

WindowsmacOS


In Windows, use File Explorer to browse folders, open files, copy or move items, and create new folders. You can open File Explorer from the taskbar or by searching for “File Explorer” from the Start menu.
A Windows computer commonly has drives identified by letters. The main drive is often C:. A path might look like this:
C:\Users\Alex\Documents\CIS_351\Week_01
The backslash (\) separates the folders in a Windows path.


In macOS, use Finder to browse folders, open files, copy or move items, and create new folders. Finder is available from the Dock.
The main storage volume is commonly accessed through the startup disk, and user files are often stored in the user’s home folder. A path might look like this:
/Users/alex/Documents/CIS_351/Week_01
The forward slash (/) separates folders in a macOS path.




A note about paths
A file path identifies where a file or folder is located. It is similar to an address: it tells the computer how to reach a particular item within the folder hierarchy.
For example, these paths refer to a folder named Week_01, but they use the conventions of different operating systems:

Windows: C:\Users\Alex\Documents\CIS_351\Week_01
macOS: /Users/alex/Documents/CIS_351/Week_01

The paths above are examples; the actual username and folder locations on your computer may differ.


Viewing the path in macOS Finder
Finder does not always show the full path to the current folder by default. To display the Path Bar:

Open a Finder window.
Click View in the menu bar.
Select Show Path Bar.

The Path Bar appears at the bottom of the Finder window and shows the folders leading to the current location. This can help you confirm where a file is stored.


Common folders
You will often encounter folders such as:

Desktop — items placed on the desktop.
Documents — a common location for documents and personal projects.
Downloads — files downloaded from a browser or other application.
Pictures — images and photographs.

Windows and macOS may provide additional folders and cloud-storage locations. Do not assume that every computer stores files in exactly the same place. When saving work for this course, choose the appropriate course or project folder and check the location before saving.

title: Section 0.1: Files, Folders, and File Types
text:
3. File Names and File Extensions

What is a filename?
A filename is the name used to identify a file. For example, in week_01_lecture.qmd, the filename is week_01_lecture.qmd.
Good filenames describe the contents of a file and make it easier to distinguish one version or assignment from another.
For this course, use these conventions unless an assignment specifies otherwise:

Use lowercase letters in filenames.
Use underscores (_) instead of spaces to separate words.
Choose names that describe the file’s contents.
Include the appropriate extension.
Avoid vague names such as stuff, newfile, or final_final.

For example, prefer week_02_lecture.qmd over Week 2 Lecture final.qmd.


What is a file extension?
A file extension is the suffix at the end of a filename, usually consisting of a period followed by letters. It often indicates the file’s format or the application commonly used to open it.
Examples:








Extension
Common file type
Typical use




.txt
Plain-text file
Notes or unformatted text


.pdf
Portable Document Format
Documents designed to preserve layout


.docx
Microsoft Word document
Word-processing documents


.xlsx
Microsoft Excel workbook
Spreadsheets with worksheets and formulas


.csv
Comma-separated values
Tabular data stored as text


.png
PNG image
Screenshots, figures, and other images


.jpg or .jpeg
JPEG image
Photographs and other compressed images


.html
HTML document
Web pages


.R
R script
Code written in R


.qmd
Quarto Markdown document
Source document that can be rendered to formats such as HTML or PDF



An extension is a useful clue, but it does not guarantee that a file is valid or safe. Also, changing a filename’s extension does not convert the file to a different format. For example, renaming data.csv to data.xlsx does not turn a CSV file into an Excel workbook.


File extensions and applications
Different applications work with different file formats. For example:

You can use Excel to open an .xlsx workbook.
You can open a .csv file in Excel or a text editor.
You can edit an .R file in a code editor such as Positron or RStudio.
You can write a .qmd file in a Quarto-compatible editor and render it into an output format.

Some file types can be opened by more than one application. Your computer’s default application determines which app opens a file when you double-click it. You can usually choose another application from the file’s context menu.

title: Section 0.1: Files, Folders, and File Types
text:
4. Showing File Extensions
Some computers hide familiar file extensions in their file-management windows. As a result, you might see penguins rather than penguins.csv. Showing extensions makes it easier to identify file types and confirm that files have the expected names.

WindowsmacOS


In current versions of Windows 11:

Open File Explorer.
Select View.
Select Show.
Turn on File name extensions.

The full filenames should now display extensions such as .csv, .xlsx, and .qmd. The precise menu layout may vary by Windows version.


To show extensions in Finder:

Open Finder.
In the menu bar, select Finder and then Settings (called Preferences in some older macOS versions).
Open the Advanced section.
Enable Show all filename extensions.

Finder should now display extensions for files when they are available. The precise wording may vary by macOS version.




Important caution when renaming files
When renaming a file, be careful not to remove or change its extension unintentionally. If you change penguins.csv to penguins.txt, the file’s contents may still be CSV data even though its name now suggests a text file. Some applications may no longer recognize the file as expected.
To convert a file, use the appropriate application’s Save As or Export function rather than simply changing the extension.

title: Section 0.1: Files, Folders, and File Types
text:
5. Creating and Managing Folders
A simple folder structure can make course work easier to manage. For example, you might keep each week’s lecture materials and data in a separate folder, or use a project folder with subfolders for data, scripts, and outputs.

WindowsmacOS


In File Explorer:

Navigate to the location where you want the folder.
Right-click an empty area of the folder window.
Select New and then Folder.
Type a name and press Enter.

You can also use the New button in File Explorer when it is available.


In Finder:

Navigate to the location where you want the folder.
Open the File menu and select New Folder, or use the Finder’s available New Folder command.
Type a name and press Return.

You can also create a folder from the context menu in many Finder views.




Moving and copying files
Copying creates another copy of a file or folder, while moving changes its location. Both operations are available through the file manager’s menus and keyboard shortcuts.
Before moving or renaming files used in a data analysis project, consider whether another file refers to their original locations. For example, a script that reads data/penguins.csv may stop working if you move the CSV file without updating the script or its path.


Keep project files together
For reproducible work, it is often best to keep related data, code, and documentation in a common project folder. A project might look like this:
penguin_analysis/
├── data/
│   └── penguins.csv
├── scripts/
│   └── clean_data.R
├── reports/
│   └── analysis.qmd
└── output/
    └── summary_table.csv
This is only an example. Use a structure that fits the project and any instructions provided for the course. Avoid creating many layers of folders unless they make the project easier to navigate.

title: Section 0.1: Files, Folders, and File Types
text:
6. Practical File-Management Habits
Good file management is not just about knowing where files are stored. It also involves developing consistent habits.

Check where you are saving. Before saving or downloading a file, confirm the destination folder.
Use descriptive names. A name such as penguin_bill_lengths.csv is more informative than data2.csv.
Keep raw data unchanged. When possible, preserve the original data and save cleaned or modified versions separately.
Separate inputs from outputs. Keep source data, scripts, reports, and generated results organized.
Use consistent naming conventions. Lowercase filenames and underscores can make names easier to work with in code.
Be careful with extensions. Do not assume that renaming a file changes its format.
Check paths when something goes wrong. If an application cannot find a file, verify the folder location and filename.

These habits help prevent common errors and make it easier for other people to follow your work.

Summary
Files store information, while folders organize files and other folders into a hierarchy. Windows uses File Explorer and commonly represents paths with drive letters and backslashes; macOS uses Finder and commonly represents paths with forward slashes. A file path identifies an item’s location, and a file extension often indicates its format or the applications that can open it.
For this course, use descriptive filenames, lowercase letters, and underscores as word separators. Keep related project files organized, check where you save them, and remember that changing a file’s extension does not convert its contents to another format.

title: Section 2.1: Introduction to Quarto Docs
text:
1. Opening A New Quarto Document
To open a new Quarto document, click the New icon on the top left corner of Position and select New File…. This will prompt another dropdown menu in the top center of Positron. Select Quarto Document.







Warning



If you opened a new Quarto document but do not see the template, then you may need to hide the lower panel. You can do this by CtrlCtrl + jj in Windows or commandcommand + jj in macOS.




2. The YAML Header
Any new Quarto document includes a document header called YAML header. YAML lets us set options to how we want the document to look. The YAML header is enclosed by two sets of --- (lines 1 and 4) and it is within this set of --- we will specify our YAML mappings.


Untitled-1.qmd

---
title: "Untitled"
format: html
---

Rewrite your YAML header so it looks like


Untitled-1.qmd

---
title: "CIS 351: Week X Lecture Y"
subtitle: "Today's Topic"
author: "Your Name"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---







WarningYAML Syntax




Be sure that your code looks exactly like mine. Except for the text inside quotation marks, you must follow the same punctuation and capitalization as shown above.
There is one indent in front of html: on line 6 and two indents in front of embed-resources: true on line 7.



Although this is optional, but it is a good idea to check the Render on Save box so Positron will automatically save the file for you whenever it renders the Quarto document.







3. Saving the Quarto Document
To save the current Quarto document, go to the top menu bar and click on File, then select Save As…. A new window will open where you can to navigate to the appropriate folder (Week X, Homework, etc). If the Quarto document is lecture notes, then use the file name week_x_lecture_y.qmd. If it is a homework assignment, then use the file name assignment_x_last_name.qmd.






ConventionConvention




If you are using a Mac, make sure that your file name ends with .qmd.
Only use lowercase letters in file names, and always use _ as the word separator. For example, week_x_lecture_y.qmd, not Week x lecture y.qmd





4. Writing Content in the Quarto Document
For the most part, content in a Quarto document are written in Quarto markdown (which is why Quarto documents use the .qmd file extension). Quarto markdown is a derivative of the markdown language.
